Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The government is warning that taking the psoriasis drug Raptiva could result in serious brain infection and even death. Raptiva may cause a serious brain infection called progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The Food and Drug Administration cited three confirmed cases, and a possible fourth, of people diagnosed with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) after being treated with Raptiva. "Three of those patients have died," the FDA said in a public health advisory. "All four patients were treated with the drug for more than three years." None was receiving other treatments that suppress the immune system. Raptiva's product labeling was revised in October to highlight a boxed warning about the risks of life-threatening infections, including PML. "At that time, the FDA directed Genentech, the manufacturer, to develop a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) to include a medication guide to educate patients about the drug's risks," the FDA's advisory says. In the advisory, issued Thursday, the FDA highlighted the confirmed cases and promised to "take appropriate steps" to ensure that Raptiva's risks do not outweigh its benefits. The FDA also said it will ensure that patients "are clearly informed of the signs and symptoms of PML" and that health care professionals "carefully monitor patients for the possible development of PML." Overseas, the European Medicines Agency has gone further, recommending that no new prescriptions for Raptiva be issued and that patients taking the drug talk to their doctors about an alternative. On Thursday it asked the European Commission to make that recommendation legally binding. The group's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use determined "that the benefits of Raptiva no longer outweigh its risks, because of safety concerns, including the occurrence of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in patients taking the medicine." It said patients who have been treated with the drug should be "closely monitored for neurological symptoms and symptoms of infection." "Patients who are currently taking Raptiva should not stop treatment abruptly, but should make an appointment with their doctor to discuss the most appropriate replacement treatment," the agency said. Raptiva, a once-weekly injection for adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, works by suppressing T-cells -- cells that help fight infection -- in the immune system. Those cells cause the skin inflammation associated with psoriasis. By suppressing T-cells, Raptiva "decreases the function of the immune system, which increases a patient's susceptibility to infections," the FDA said. The National Institutes of Health says the prognosis for PML "remains grim; the disease usually lasts for months and 80 percent die within the first six months, although spontaneous improvement has been reported. Those who survive PML can be left with severe neurological disabilities." Around 6 million to 7 million Americans have psoriasis, which is incurable, the NIH says.

Raptiva may cause progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a serious brain infection. The Food and Drug Administration cited three confirmed cases—and a possible fourth—of PML among people treated with the drug.

“Three of those patients have died,” the FDA said in a public health advisory. “All four patients were treated with the drug for more than three years.” None of the patients was receiving other treatments that suppress the immune system.

Raptiva’s product labeling was revised in October to include a boxed warning highlighting the risk of life-threatening infections, including PML.

In the advisory, issued Thursday, the FDA highlighted the confirmed cases and pledged to “take appropriate steps” to ensure that Raptiva’s risks do not outweigh its benefits. The agency also said it would ensure that patients “are clearly informed of the signs and symptoms of PML” and that health care professionals “carefully monitor patients for the possible development of PML.”

Overseas, the European Medicines Agency has taken further action, recommending that no new prescriptions for Raptiva be issued and that patients taking the drug consult their doctors about an alternative. On Thursday, the agency asked the European Commission to make that recommendation legally binding.

The agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use determined “that the benefits of Raptiva no longer outweigh its risks, because of safety concerns, including the occurrence of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in patients taking the medicine.”

It said patients who have been treated with the drug should be “closely monitored for neurological symptoms and symptoms of infection.”

“Patients who are currently taking Raptiva should not stop treatment abruptly, but should make an appointment with their doctor to discuss the most appropriate replacement treatment,” the agency said.

Raptiva, a once-weekly injection for adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, works by suppressing T-cells—immune-system cells that help fight infection. These cells also cause the skin inflammation associated with psoriasis.

By suppressing T-cells, Raptiva “decreases the function of the immune system, which increases a patient’s susceptibility to infections,” the FDA said.

According to the National Institutes of Health, the prognosis for PML “remains grim; the disease usually lasts for months and 80 percent die within the first six months, although spontaneous improvement has been reported. Those who survive PML can be left with severe neurological disabilities.”

About 6 million to 7 million Americans have psoriasis, an incurable condition, the NIH says.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Federal health officials are cautioning that Raptiva, a medication used to treat psoriasis, may lead to a dangerous brain infection and can be fatal.

The Food and Drug Administration reported three verified cases—and one additional suspected case—of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, or PML, among patients who had received Raptiva. Three of the four patients died. Each had used the medicine for longer than three years, and none was undergoing any other treatment that weakened the immune system.

In October, Raptiva’s labeling was updated with a prominent boxed warning emphasizing the possibility of potentially fatal infections, including PML. At that point, the FDA instructed the drug’s manufacturer, Genentech, to create a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy, known as a REMS. The plan was to include a medication guide informing patients about the risks associated with the drug.

In a public health notice released Thursday, the agency drew attention to the confirmed PML cases and said it would take whatever action was necessary to make certain that Raptiva’s dangers did not exceed its benefits. The FDA also said patients must receive clear information about PML symptoms and warning signs, while medical professionals should closely watch users for evidence that the infection may be developing.

European regulators have adopted a stronger position. The European Medicines Agency recommended that doctors stop issuing new Raptiva prescriptions and advised current users to consult their physicians about switching to another therapy. On Thursday, the agency asked the European Commission to give the recommendation the force of law.

The agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use concluded that Raptiva’s benefits no longer justified its risks. Its decision was based on safety issues, including PML occurring in people taking the medication. The committee said anyone who had received Raptiva should be monitored carefully for neurological problems and signs of infection.

The European agency also warned existing patients not to discontinue the medicine suddenly. Instead, they should schedule a medical appointment to determine the most suitable replacement treatment.

Raptiva is administered by injection once a week to adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis. It works by inhibiting immune-system T-cells, which normally help the body combat infection but also contribute to the skin inflammation caused by psoriasis. According to the FDA, reducing T-cell activity weakens immune function and makes patients more vulnerable to infections.

The National Institutes of Health describes the outlook for people with PML as extremely poor. The illness typically continues for several months, and 80 percent of patients die within the first six months, though some spontaneous recovery has occurred. Survivors may experience serious neurological impairments.

Psoriasis has no cure and affects approximately 6 million to 7 million people in the United States, according to the NIH.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is reviewing reports of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) in patients treated with Raptiva (efalizumab), a prescription medicine used for adults with chronic moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. PML is a rare but often fatal brain infection caused by reactivation of the JC virus, usually in people whose immune systems have been weakened. It can lead to rapidly worsening neurological problems, including confusion, vision changes, difficulty speaking or walking, weakness, and loss of coordination.

Three confirmed cases of PML and one possible case were reported among patients who had received Raptiva continuously for more than three years. Three of the patients died. None of the affected patients was known to be taking other immune-suppressing treatments at the time, raising concern that long-term exposure to Raptiva itself may increase the risk.

The FDA is evaluating the available safety information and working with the manufacturer to determine whether further regulatory action is needed. The agency had already strengthened Raptiva’s prescribing information, including prominent warnings about serious infections such as PML. It also required additional patient education, including a Medication Guide, and enhanced monitoring intended to help doctors and patients recognize neurological symptoms as early as possible.

Patients taking Raptiva should contact their healthcare professional promptly if they develop new or worsening neurological symptoms, such as confusion, dizziness, trouble talking or walking, vision problems, or weakness on one side of the body. They should not stop treatment abruptly without medical advice, because sudden discontinuation may cause psoriasis to return or worsen. Doctors should carefully reassess whether each patient should continue therapy and should discontinue the drug if PML is suspected.

European regulators reached a more restrictive conclusion. After reviewing the reported cases and the overall safety profile of Raptiva, they determined that the drug’s risks outweighed its benefits and recommended suspending its authorization. Healthcare professionals were advised not to begin treatment in new patients and to review alternatives for those already receiving the medicine. Any withdrawal from Raptiva was to be managed under medical supervision.

The reports underscore the importance of close monitoring during long-term immune-modifying treatment and of promptly reporting serious adverse effects to regulators.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about FDA warnings that the psoriasis drug Raptiva may cause progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and death.
counterfactuals.output:
## FDA warns psoriasis drug Raptiva linked to rare brain infection, deaths

**WASHINGTON** — The U.S. Food and Drug Administration warned that the psoriasis drug Raptiva has been linked to cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, or PML, a rare and often fatal brain infection.

The agency said patients taking Raptiva, known generically as efalizumab, faced a potential risk of PML, particularly after long-term treatment. Several reported patients died after developing the infection.

PML is caused by activation of the JC virus, which is common but typically remains dormant in healthy people. In patients with weakened immune systems, the virus can damage the brain’s white matter, leading to worsening weakness, vision problems, confusion, difficulty speaking and loss of coordination. There is no known cure.

The FDA advised doctors to closely monitor patients for new neurological symptoms and to stop Raptiva if PML is suspected. Patients were urged to contact their physicians immediately if they experienced unusual weakness, changes in vision, confusion or problems with balance and movement.

Raptiva suppresses parts of the immune system and was approved for adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. Regulators cautioned patients not to discontinue the medication without first consulting a health care professional.

The warning was later followed by a voluntary withdrawal of Raptiva from the U.S. market in 2009.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the latest U.S. and European regulatory actions concerning Raptiva, including confirmed PML cases, fatalities, patient guidance, and how the drug affects the immune system.
counterfactuals.output:
### Regulatory status and cases

**United States — FDA**
- In **February 2009**, the FDA warned of **three confirmed cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)** and **one additional suspected case** in patients taking Raptiva (efalizumab), generally after more than three years of treatment.
- Across those four reports, **three patients died**; not every fatal case had been classified as confirmed PML at the time of the warning.
- In **April 2009**, Genentech announced a phased voluntary U.S. withdrawal, with distribution ending by **June 8, 2009**. Physicians were told not to start new patients and to transition existing patients to alternatives.

**European Union — EMA**
- In **February 2009**, the EMA recommended suspension of Raptiva’s marketing authorization because its modest psoriasis benefit no longer outweighed the risks, particularly PML and other serious infections.
- The EMA cited **three confirmed PML cases, two of them fatal**, plus another suspected case.
- The European Commission subsequently suspended the authorization, and the product was ultimately withdrawn from the EU market.

The different fatality figures reflect how the regulators classified the four reports at the time: the FDA reported three deaths overall, while the EMA specifically described two fatal **confirmed** PML cases.

### Patient guidance

Patients were advised to:
- **Contact their prescriber promptly** to arrange another psoriasis treatment.
- **Not stop Raptiva abruptly without medical supervision**, because psoriasis could rebound or worsen severely.
- Seek urgent evaluation for possible PML symptoms, including new or worsening:
  - weakness or clumsiness,
  - difficulty walking or speaking,
  - vision changes,
  - confusion, memory problems, or personality changes.
- Remain under observation after stopping, since PML or other infections may become apparent after treatment ends.

### How Raptiva affects immunity

Raptiva is a monoclonal antibody that binds **CD11a**, part of the **LFA-1** molecule on T lymphocytes. It interferes with T-cell activation, adhesion, and movement from the bloodstream into tissues, reducing the immune-driven inflammation of psoriasis. That same action weakens immune surveillance, allowing latent infections—most notably **JC virus**, the cause of PML—to reactivate.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed health news article explaining the risks associated with long-term Raptiva use for moderate to severe plaque psoriasis.
counterfactuals.output:
# Raptiva’s Long-Term Risks: Why the Psoriasis Drug Was Withdrawn

**Raptiva, once prescribed for moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, was removed from the market after prolonged treatment was linked to a rare but often fatal brain infection. The drug is no longer an approved psoriasis therapy in the United States or European Union.**

Raptiva, the brand name for **efalizumab**, was a weekly injectable biologic used in adults with chronic moderate to severe plaque psoriasis who were candidates for systemic treatment or phototherapy. By interfering with the activation and movement of T cells, it could reduce the immune activity that contributes to psoriasis.

That immune suppression, however, also impaired the body’s ability to control certain infections. The most serious concern was **progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy**, or PML—a rare neurological disease caused by reactivation of the JC virus.

## PML was the central long-term safety concern

The JC virus is common and usually remains dormant without causing illness. In people whose immune defenses are weakened, the virus can infect cells in the brain and damage myelin, the protective covering around nerves.

PML can progress rapidly and may cause:

- Increasing weakness or clumsiness, sometimes on one side of the body
- Difficulty walking or loss of coordination
- Vision changes
- Problems speaking or understanding language
- Confusion, memory loss, or personality changes
- Seizures

There is no reliably effective cure for PML. The condition can lead to severe, permanent disability or death.

Reports of PML emerged among people who had received Raptiva continuously, generally for **about three years or longer**. Although the number of identified cases was small, the consequences were grave and there was no established way to predict which treated patients would develop the infection.

In 2009, regulators concluded that Raptiva’s risks outweighed its benefits. The manufacturer voluntarily withdrew it from the U.S. market, and its marketing authorization in the European Union was suspended. Patients were advised not to stop abruptly without medical supervision because psoriasis could rebound or worsen.

## Serious infections beyond PML

Because Raptiva altered T-cell function, long-term treatment could increase susceptibility to other infections. Reported concerns included serious bacterial and viral infections, such as:

- Pneumonia
- Sepsis
- Meningitis
- Opportunistic infections that generally occur in immunocompromised people

The risk could be greater in people with an existing infection, a weakened immune system, or exposure to other immunosuppressive medicines. At the time the drug was marketed, its labeling warned clinicians to evaluate patients for infections and discontinue treatment when serious infection developed.

As with many immune-modifying drugs, vaccination required special consideration. **Live vaccines could pose a safety risk**, while the immune response to other vaccines might be reduced.

## Blood disorders and immune complications

Raptiva was also associated with potentially serious abnormalities involving blood cells.

### Thrombocytopenia

Some patients developed **low platelet counts**, which can impair clotting. Warning signs include:

- Unusual bruising
- Tiny red or purple spots under the skin
- Bleeding from the gums or nose
- Blood in urine or stool
- Prolonged bleeding after minor injuries

Periodic platelet monitoring was recommended because severe thrombocytopenia could occur after treatment began.

### Hemolytic anemia

Rare reports described **immune-mediated hemolytic anemia**, in which the immune system destroys red blood cells. Possible symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath, rapid heartbeat, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin and eyes.

## Neurological and inflammatory reactions

Raptiva’s safety information included reports of neurological disorders and inflammatory reactions. In addition to PML, these included conditions such as transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and other demyelinating illnesses.

Some patients also experienced an “arthritis event,” with new or worsening joint pain and swelling. Hypersensitivity reactions—including hives, swelling, breathing difficulty, or anaphylaxis—were another potential risk.

More common adverse effects, particularly around the first few doses, included headache, fever, chills, nausea, muscle pain, and back pain.

## Psoriasis could rebound after discontinuation

Stopping Raptiva could be followed by a return of psoriasis, sometimes worse than it had been before treatment. This phenomenon, often described as **rebound psoriasis**, could lead to extensive or unstable disease and require prompt transition to another therapy.

That concern was especially important during the 2009 withdrawal. Regulators and the manufacturer recommended that clinicians arrange alternative treatment rather than have patients discontinue the drug without a plan.

## Cancer risk was another theoretical concern

Long-term suppression or alteration of immune surveillance can potentially affect the body’s ability to detect abnormal cells. Malignancies were reported during Raptiva’s clinical development and post-marketing use, although it was not always possible to determine whether the medicine directly caused them.

The uncertainty added to concerns about prolonged exposure, particularly because psoriasis generally requires years or decades of management.

## What former Raptiva users should know today

Raptiva has not been routinely available for many years, and **PML associated with the drug was primarily a concern during active, prolonged immune suppression**. A former patient who is currently well should not assume that new symptoms are related to remote exposure.

Nevertheless, anyone with a history of Raptiva use should make sure it remains in their medical record. New neurological symptoms—especially progressive weakness, coordination problems, vision changes, confusion, or speech difficulties—require prompt medical evaluation, regardless of their suspected cause.

Patients should not use leftover Raptiva or obtain it from unregulated sources.

## Safer treatment choices now available

Psoriasis treatment has changed substantially since Raptiva was withdrawn. Current options include phototherapy, conventional systemic medicines, and biologics targeting pathways such as tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-17, interleukin-23, and interleukin-12/23.

These treatments have their own risks, including infection and other immune effects, but they are supported by current prescribing guidance and ongoing safety monitoring. Choice of therapy depends on psoriasis severity, joint involvement, other medical conditions, pregnancy plans, previous treatments, and individual preferences.

**Bottom line:** Raptiva demonstrated how suppressing immune-cell activity can improve psoriasis while creating serious long-term hazards. Its association with PML—particularly after years of continuous use—ultimately led regulators and the manufacturer to remove it from the market. Anyone who believes they are still using efalizumab, or who has concerns about prior exposure, should consult a dermatologist or other qualified clinician rather than changing treatment independently.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the FDA public health advisory about Raptiva and compare it with the European Medicines Agency’s recommendation to halt new prescriptions.
counterfactuals.output:
## Raptiva safety actions: FDA vs. European Medicines Agency

**Raptiva (efalizumab)** was a biologic medicine used to treat adults with chronic moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. The regulatory concern was **progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)**, a rare, often fatal brain infection caused by reactivation of the JC virus during immune suppression.

### FDA public health advisory

On **February 19, 2009**, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced that it had received reports of:

- **Three confirmed cases of PML**, all fatal, and  
- **One additional possible case**.

The patients had generally received Raptiva for **more than three years**, and none was reported to be taking another immunosuppressive therapy at the time. The FDA emphasized that there was **no known effective treatment for PML**.

At that stage, however, the FDA **did not order a suspension or tell physicians to stop initiating treatment**. Instead, it advised:

- Prescribers to reassess Raptiva’s risks and benefits;
- Close monitoring for new neurological symptoms, such as confusion, weakness, vision or speech problems, and impaired coordination;
- Prompt evaluation and discontinuation if PML was suspected; and
- Patients not to stop Raptiva without medical guidance, partly because abrupt withdrawal could cause psoriasis to worsen or rebound.

The FDA was continuing to evaluate whether further regulatory action was needed. Raptiva already carried a boxed warning concerning serious infections, including PML.

### European Medicines Agency recommendation

On the same date, the European Medicines Agency’s scientific committee, the **CHMP**, concluded that Raptiva’s benefits no longer outweighed its risks and recommended **suspension of its European marketing authorization**.

Pending the European Commission’s formal decision, the agency advised that:

- **No new patients should be prescribed Raptiva**;
- Physicians should review patients already receiving it and arrange appropriate alternative treatment;
- Discontinuation should be managed carefully because of the possibility of psoriasis rebound; and
- Patients stopping treatment should continue to be monitored for neurological symptoms and infection.

The European assessment considered not only PML but also other serious infections, including encephalitis, meningitis, sepsis, and opportunistic infections. It also judged Raptiva’s psoriasis benefit to be relatively modest and noted that alternative treatments were available.

## Main difference

| Issue | FDA advisory | EMA/CHMP recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| Immediate regulatory stance | Heightened warning and monitoring while evaluation continued | Recommended suspension of authorization |
| New prescriptions | Did not initially impose a halt | Explicitly advised no new prescriptions |
| Existing patients | Individual risk-benefit review; do not stop without medical advice | Review all patients and transition them to alternatives |
| Overall conclusion in February 2009 | Serious safety signal requiring urgent caution | Benefit-risk balance was unfavorable |

Thus, the **FDA initially took a more cautious, interim risk-management approach**, while the **EMA recommended removing Raptiva from routine use and immediately stopping initiation of new patients**.

The U.S. position later converged with Europe’s practical outcome: in **April 2009**, the manufacturer announced a voluntary phased withdrawal of Raptiva from the U.S. market, completed in **June 2009**, because of the PML risk.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
**Raptiva linked to fatal brain infections, prompting tighter safety controls**

WASHINGTON — The psoriasis drug Raptiva was linked to several cases of a rare and often fatal brain infection, leading U.S. regulators to strengthen warnings, recommend closer monitoring and require manufacturer Genentech to adopt additional risk-management measures.

Raptiva, known generically as efalizumab, was approved in 2003 as a once-weekly injectable treatment for adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis who were candidates for systemic therapy or phototherapy. The drug suppresses parts of the immune system involved in psoriasis, but that effect can also reduce the body’s ability to fight serious infections.

The Food and Drug Administration said three confirmed cases and one possible case of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, or PML, had been reported among Raptiva users. Three of the patients died. All had taken the drug for more than three years and had not been receiving other immune-suppressing treatments.

PML is caused by reactivation of the common JC virus, which usually remains dormant. In people with weakened immune systems, the virus can attack the brain’s white matter, causing rapidly worsening neurological damage. Symptoms may include weakness, loss of coordination, difficulty walking, changes in vision or speech, confusion and personality changes. There is no proven cure, and the infection can cause severe disability or death.

Regulators advised doctors to reassess periodically whether patients should remain on Raptiva, particularly after prolonged treatment, and to monitor them closely for new neurological symptoms. Treatment should be stopped if PML is suspected, followed by prompt neurological evaluation.

Patients were told not to discontinue Raptiva on their own because sudden withdrawal could cause psoriasis to flare or worsen. Anyone experiencing confusion, weakness, vision problems, speech difficulties, loss of balance or other new neurological symptoms was advised to contact a health professional immediately. Physicians were also encouraged to consider alternative psoriasis treatments.

The FDA had previously required a boxed warning describing the risks of PML and other serious infections. Genentech was also directed to implement a formal risk-evaluation and mitigation strategy, provide patients with an FDA-approved Medication Guide, improve communication about the drug’s hazards and ensure that patients and prescribers understood the need for monitoring. The company was additionally required to gather more information about the incidence and risk factors for PML.

Raptiva was subsequently withdrawn from the U.S. market in 2009 because of the PML risk and the lack of a reliable way to predict which patients would develop the infection.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
